title: Polynomial-time online sparse regression with a fixed regret exponent
formal:
Assume \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\). Do there exist a rational constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\), positive integers \(C,a\), and one uniform classical randomized online algorithm such that, for every \(d,T,b\ge1\), \(1\le k\le d\), and every fixed rational input sequence satisfying the conditions below, the algorithm observes at most \(k\) coordinates per round, uses at most \(C(d+k+T+b+2)^a\) bit operations per round including initialization, and has expected regret
\[
\mathbb E\left[\sum_{t=1}^T(\widehat y_t-y_t)^2\right]-\min_{\substack{w\in\mathbb R^d\\\|w\|_0\le k,\ \|w\|_2\le1}}\sum_{t=1}^T(\langle w,x_t\rangle-y_t)^2
\le C(d+k+2)^a T^{1-\delta}?
\]
The same constants and algorithm must work for all parameters and sequences. This historical target has a negative answer under the displayed assumption.
why: The problem separates the information needed to predict from the computation needed to identify useful features. Its negative resolution shows that allowing improper predictions does not remove the computational barrier of competing with an unknown sparse regressor.
status_note: Conditionally resolved negatively by Foster–Kale–Karloff (COLT 2016) under NP not contained in BPP, for the explicitly selected fixed-exponent regret target. The source reduction was checked against the finite-bit, equal-observation-budget formulation. This is a source and formulation review, not an independent formal verification of the full hardness theorem. sentences: The learner predicts a numerical label after inspecting at most k coordinates of each example.
Its total squared loss is compared with the best fixed k-sparse unit-norm linear predictor.
The selected target requires polynomial computation and a fixed positive saving in the exponent of the number of rounds.
A 2016 reduction shows that such a learner would place NP inside BPP.
The historical target is therefore archived under the stated complexity assumption, without claiming every slower sublinear rate impossible.

definitions:
For an integer \(d\ge1\), write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). The sequence consists of \(T\) pairs \((x_t,y_t)\in\mathbb Q^d\times\mathbb Q\) with \(\|x_t\|_2\le1\) and \(-1\le y_t\le1\). Each rational is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator; its complete encoding has length at most the supplied integer \(b\). The entire sequence is fixed before the learner's random bits are drawn, but is hidden from it. The learner initially receives only \(d,k,T,b\), in binary. It has no sampling or evaluation access to undisclosed entries or future examples.

In round \(t\), the learner first chooses a set \(S_t\subseteq[d]\) of at most \(k\) indices, using only its parameters, internal random bits and previously received feedback. All indices are chosen before any coordinate of \(x_t\) is disclosed. It then receives precisely \((x_t(i))_{i\in S_t}\), emits a rational prediction \(\widehat y_t\in[-1,1]\), and receives the true label \(y_t\). It receives no additional features after predicting. Its squared loss is \((\widehat y_t-y_t)^2\). The model permits different observed sets in different rounds and arbitrary, possibly nonlinear prediction rules on the observed data; it does not require the learner to output a sparse weight vector.

The comparator is a single fixed real vector \(w\) selected after the full sequence is known. Here \(\langle w,x\rangle=\sum_iw_ix_i\), \(\|w\|_2=(\sum_iw_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\|w\|_0\) is the number of nonzero coordinates. The comparator has the same sparsity budget \(k\), not an observation budget that varies with time. The displayed minimum exists because the allowed vectors form a finite union of compact coordinate balls. Expectation is solely over the learner's independent fair random bits, for each individual fixed sequence.

Computation is on a probabilistic multitape Turing machine. Reading and writing parameters, query indices, disclosed rationals and predictions, arithmetic, memory operations, and generation of random bits are charged. Initialization is included in the first round's bound, and every execution satisfies the time bound. Each coordinate reply is the explicitly encoded rational; it is not a unit-cost exact-real arithmetic oracle. The horizon is known, all polynomial exponents are independent of every input parameter, and there is no advice or computational oracle. The regret coefficient is polynomial in \(d,k\) and independent of the precision bound \(b\).

The assumption \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) says that some language having polynomial-length witnesses verifiable in deterministic polynomial bit time has no randomized polynomial-bit-time decision algorithm with error at most \(1/3\) on each input. Equivalently, Boolean 3-CNF satisfiability has no such randomized algorithm. The fixed positive \(\delta\) is chosen before all input parameters. The selected statement concerns a polynomial saving in the horizon exponent; it does not assert that every unspecified \(o(T)\) convergence rate is excluded.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence statement under its stated complexity assumption. A negative answer must exclude all fixed positive regret-exponent savings with polynomial dimension dependence in the stated limited-observation bit model. The known conditional negative result supports archival; no completed Lean formalization is claimed.

source_formulation.text: The 2014 question asks for polynomial computation and poly(d,k) times o(T) regret, allowing some relaxed observation budgets. The selected historical target uses the explicit fixed-exponent no-regret convention in the 2016 resolution and preserves the original equal k-coordinate observation budget. This quantitative restriction and conditional archival are the announced editorial recommendation after an unanswered optional scope question. context_blocks.text: The original task restricts feature access during prediction, unlike batch attribute-efficient learning that may inspect all features at test time.

The 2016 paper explicitly resolves the computational question for a regret bound with a fixed positive power saving. Its lower bound even allows a logarithmic factor more observed coordinates than the comparator uses.

The lower-bound examples can be generated independently from one fixed distribution; their hardness is not caused solely by an adversary reacting to the learner. Polynomial algorithms under additional regularity assumptions on the examples address a different domain.

checked_sources: Read the complete 2014 question and the 2016 model, Reduction 1, Theorem 2 proof and conclusions.

For the finite-bit specialization, the proof permits x=sign times a set-cover row divided by d, y=sign/(dk), and comparator weights 1/k on an exact cover. Their norms are at most one; an uncovered row gives expected loss at least 1/(m d^2 k^2), still inverse polynomial. This replaces the source square-root normalization without changing the reduction.
Bounded later checks distinguish algorithms requiring RIP or other data regularity from the unrestricted sequence target.
